title: Virome City
text:
The route
Human viromes are tiny, noisy, and sample-dependent. Small early choices — which sample, which enrichment, DNA or RNA, which pipeline — quietly decide what you can see at the end.
This guide makes those choices legible.
Four questions, in order — then the tool that turns your answers into a method.

title: Virome City
text:
District 1 How should I think about viruses?
What a virus is made of, and the three questions that decide your method: who it infects, what genome it carries, and what state it is in.


Why Why the virome matters
Short comic-style stories of how studying viromes has shaped human health — evolution, ecology, medicine.


Where Where viruses hide
Everywhere, but tiny. How the way you search changes across the body — and where the noise comes from.


How-to How to design the experiment
Convert, enrich, sequence, analyze. What all of the above means for your protocol, from sampling to bioinformatics.


Then the tool Fivi’s Kitchen
Pick your sample, your target and your experience. Fivi cooks a method plan for your exact case — including the times when the honest answer is “you don’t need metagenomics at all.”

title: How should I think about viruses?
text:
If you’re coming from bacterial genomics or metagenomics, it’s tempting to assume viruses can be studied the same way.
They can’t.
Viruses don’t follow a single experimental or computational workflow. Their biology is extraordinarily diverse, and every methodological decision begins with understanding what kind of virus you’re actually looking for.
To understand why viruses require different approaches, you first need to understand how they are built.
crumbs: 2  How should I think about viruses?

title: How should I think about viruses?
text:
What are they made of?



1 Genome — the nucleic acid (DNA or RNA); the instructions you sequence.
2 Capsid — the protein shell that packages and protects the genome.
3 Surface / attachment proteins — how it recognizes and enters a host.
4 Envelope (optional) — a lipid membrane borrowed from the host; only some viruses have one.








Figure 2.1



Their structure is simple: a piece of genetic material — RNA or DNA, single- or double-stranded — wrapped in a protein shell called the capsid. Some viruses add an outer lipid envelope, stolen from the host and studded with surface proteins that help them latch onto host cells (like a coronavirus’s spikes).


In Virome City, biological questions come before methodological ones.


Viral diversity can feel overwhelming. Instead of memorizing every viral family or taxonomic group, let’s organize this diversity around three questions:

Who do they infect?
What kind of genome do they carry?
What is their biological state?
crumbs: 2  How should I think about viruses?

title: How should I think about viruses?
text:
Who do they infect?

Every virus depends on a host.
Unlike cellular organisms, viruses cannot replicate on their own. They lack the machinery needed to copy their genomes and instead rely on another living organism to do the job. That organism is the host.



Don’t look for us on the tree. We aren’t a branch of it — we’re something that happens to every branch. I infect bacteria; others infect archaea, and others infect you.








Figure 2.2





Understanding the host is one of the first questions in viral research because it shapes where viruses are found, how they evolve, and which experimental and computational approaches are most appropriate.
crumbs: 2  How should I think about viruses?

title: How should I think about viruses?
section: What kind of genome do they carry?
text:
What kind of genome do they carry?

Unlike other cellular organisms, viruses don’t all use the same genetic material. Their genomes may be DNA or RNA, and each can be either single- or double-stranded.





RNA


DNA


One strand (ss)



ssRNA
coronavirus, influenza



ssDNA
Anelloviridae (TTV), Microviridae


Two strands (ds)



dsRNA
rotavirus



dsDNA
most phages, herpes, adenovirus




Before you ever sequence a sample, these differences determine which workflows are appropriate — and which ones will fail.

title: How should I think about viruses?
text:
How do they exist?

Not every virus exists as a free viral particle.
Some remain integrated within their host’s genome for part — or even all — of their lifecycle.



state · 1

state: exogenous
Exogenous
A free particle that infects from outside — the classic virion.


→ can integrate into the host genome →


state · 2

state: endogenous
Endogenous
Genome written into the host’s DNA — inherited or long-resident, not a free particle.



endogenous forms, by host



Prophages bacterial host



Proviruses archaeal host



ERVs eukaryotic host

retroviral non-retroviral (EVEs)







Their biological state determines how they are detected — and whether they are detected at all.


ERVs descend from retroviruses, which integrate into the host genome as a normal step in their lifecycle. Non-retroviral EVEs come from viruses that never integrate at all — fragments captured by accident and then inherited. The distinction matters for detection: a search built around retroviral signatures will not find the second kind.



Don’t overlook this axis. Biological state may determine whether your workflow finds me at all. We’ll put this into practice in the How-to district.
